question: Why is the approach and landing the most demanding manoeuvre for a pilot?

options.text: The aircraft is at its heaviest weight
All three axes and the airspeed must be controlled together
The autopilot cannot be used at all in this phase of flight
The radio aids are least accurate there

explanation: Landing needs simultaneous control in pitch, roll and yaw plus speed control through power changes, which is why automating it is demanding too.

question: About what sink rate should be achieved just before touchdown?
explanation: The pilot, or the autoland, aims to reduce the sink rate to about 2 ft per second before touchdown.

question: Over the final approach and flare, airspeed is reduced from about:
explanation: Airspeed is reduced from about 1.3 VS to about 1.15 VS by progressively reducing engine power.

question: What is "de-crabbing"?

options.text: Lowering the nose onto the runway
Yawing to remove the drift angle before touchdown
Correcting the heading after a go-around from the runway

explanation: Before touchdown the wings are levelled and the aircraft yawed to align with the runway, removing the drift angle: drift kick-off or de-crabbing.

question: How must an automatic landing system compare with a pilot?

options.text: It must give better guidance and control than required of the pilot
It may be less accurate, but more consistent
It needs only to fly the approach, and not the landing itself
It must match the average pilot's performance

explanation: A system that takes over from the pilot must be able to provide guidance and control better than that required of the pilot.

question: What is an auto-approach?

options.text: An approach with the autothrottle off
An automatic approach with the pilot landing manually at DH
An approach flown on the flight director only, with the autopilot off
An automatic landing without a flare

explanation: All procedures are as for an autoland, but at decision height the pilot takes over and lands manually, for example where ground equipment does not allow autoland.

question: Which of these is an objective of an autoland system?

options.text: It must never disconnect in flight
It must work without ground aids
It must warn of a passive failure
It must fly the take-off as well

explanation: The system must not disturb the flight path after an active malfunction, have enough authority, warn of a passive failure, and allow the manoeuvre to be completed after a failure.

question: How many independent autopilots does an autoland system need as a minimum?

options.text: One, with a yaw damper and two radio altimeters
Two, able to follow ILS signals

explanation: Autoland needs at least two independent autopilots able to follow ILS signals, two independent radio altimeters and a category 3 ILS on the ground.

question: How many radio altimeters does an autoland system require?

options.text: None; it uses the glide slope only

explanation: Two independent radio altimeters give accurate height above the ground for the flare and other height-based stages.

question: Which ground installation does autoland require?
explanation: An autoland needs a category 3 ILS ground installation at the airport.

question: What does fail-passive mean for an autoland system?

options.text: A failure is not shown to the crew
A failure has no effect on the autoland
A failure ends the autoland without a dangerous deviation
A failure makes the aircraft go around automatically at once

explanation: A fail-passive (fail-soft) system withstands a failure without endangering the passengers or causing excessive flight path deviations, but loses its ability to complete the automatic landing.

question: What is the minimum number of autopilots for fail-passive capability?
explanation: Fail-passive operation needs at least two autopilots, so that one can monitor the other.

question: What does fail-operational mean?

options.text: A failure leaves the pilot to flare and land manually
A failure disconnects the autopilot safely
A failure produces only a warning
A failure does not stop the system completing the landing

explanation: A fail-operational (fail-active) system withstands a failure without affecting its overall function or degrading performance beyond the autoland limits.

question: What is the normal minimum number of autopilots for fail-operational capability?
explanation: Fail-operational normally needs three autopilots. Two may be enough if each channel has suitable duplicate monitoring.

question: How can a fail-operational capability be achieved with only two autopilots?

options.text: With duplicate monitoring of each channel
By using the flight director as a third channel
By adding a third radio altimeter
It cannot be achieved with two

explanation: Two autopilots can give fail-operational capability provided each channel has suitable duplicate monitoring.

question: What does a LAND 2 annunciation signify?
explanation: LAND 2 means dual redundancy of engaged flight control computers, sensors and servos, giving fail-passive operation.

question: What does LAND 3 signify?

options.text: Dual redundancy of computers: fail-passive operation

explanation: LAND 3 means triple redundancy of power sources, flight control computers, sensors and servos, giving fail-operational operation.

question: What is the alert height in automatic landing operations?

options.text: The height at which the autothrottle retards
The height at which the flare begins
The height above which a failure means a go-around
The decision height used for a category I approach

explanation: Above the alert height a failure of the fail-operational system leads to a go-around. Below it, the approach and landing continue automatically after a single failure.

question: Below alert height, one channel of a fail-operational autoland fails. What happens?
explanation: That is what fail-operational means: after a single failure below alert height the system continues and completes the landing.

question: During an approach, one channel of a triplex autoland fails above alert height. To which status does the system revert?
explanation: With one of three channels lost, two remain, giving dual redundancy: fail-passive operation, annunciated LAND 2.

question: During the cruise and initial approach, how does a triple-channel autoland system operate?

options.text: With two channels and one monitor

explanation: During cruise and the initial approach the system operates as a single channel, controlling pitch and roll and giving flight director commands.

question: What does pressing APPR on the flight control panel do in a multi-channel autoland?

options.text: Disconnects the autopilot automatically at decision height
Arms the other channels and the LOC and G/S modes

explanation: Pressing APPR arms the remaining channels and also arms the localizer and glide slope modes. The off-line channels receive the outer loop signals and compare continuously.

question: From what height does the radio altimeter typically provide vertical guidance?
explanation: The radio altimeter becomes effective once the aircraft is within its operating range, typically 2500 ft.

question: In a typical dual system, what does the captain's radio altimeter also supply?
explanation: Each radio altimeter feeds its own FCC, and the captain's also provides radio altitude to the autothrottle.

question: What is the effect on autoland if one radio altimeter fails?

options.text: The system becomes fail-passive at best
There is no effect on autoland

explanation: The associated FCC (and the autothrottle if affected) must not be used for approach and landing, so a single radio altimeter failure makes the system fail-passive.

question: In dual autopilot fail-passive operation, which autopilot do the controls follow?

options.text: The one commanding the least control movement
The one commanding the most control movement at the time

explanation: During fail-passive operation the flight controls respond to the autopilot commanding the least control movement, so a runaway in one cannot drive the controls.

question: For a dual autopilot approach, by what height must the second autopilot be engaged?
explanation: Both VHF nav receivers must be tuned to the ILS and the second autopilot engaged before 800 ft RA; below that its engagement is inhibited.

question: When does the armed second autopilot engage automatically?

options.text: At glide slope capture only, at any height above 2500 ft
After LOC and G/S capture, below 1500 ft RA
At 800 ft RA, whatever has been captured
At localizer capture, at any height

explanation: Selecting the second autopilot in APP mode arms it to engage automatically after both LOC and G/S are captured and the aircraft descends below 1500 ft RA.

question: In which modes can the localizer be intercepted for an approach?

options.text: HDG SEL, CWS R or LNAV
ALT HOLD or V/S only, never LNAV

explanation: The localizer can be intercepted in HDG SEL, CWS R or LNAV. Either LOC or G/S may be captured first, though LOC first is most common.

question: On localizer capture, which autopilot status is annunciated?
explanation: At LOC capture, VOR LOC shows captured, 1 CH is annunciated for the autopilot status, the previous roll mode disengages and the aircraft tracks the localizer.

question: From which direction is glide slope capture generally preferred?
explanation: The glide slope can be captured from above or below, but capture from below is generally preferred.

question: At what deviation is the glide slope captured?
explanation: Glide slope capture occurs at 2/5 dot deviation. Localizer capture occurs not later than ½ dot.

question: At glide slope capture, which N1 limit is annunciated for the autothrottle?
explanation: At G/S capture the annunciated N1 thrust limit becomes GA, ready for a go-around.

question: After LOC and G/S capture, how can APP mode be exited?

options.text: By pressing the APP switch a second time
By selecting a new MCP altitude
By TO/GA, or disengaging A/P with both FDs off, or re-tuning

explanation: Once both are captured, APP can be exited only by pressing TOGA, disengaging the autopilot and turning both FD switches off, or re-tuning a VHF nav receiver.

question: After LOC and G/S capture, what happens if the ILS signal becomes invalid?

options.text: Nothing; the inertial data takes over
The autopilot changes to heading hold on the localizer course
The A/Ps disengage and the FD bars retract

explanation: An invalid ILS signal after capture causes the autopilots to disengage and the FD command bars to retract.

question: Below 1500 ft RA with both beams captured, which mode is armed?
explanation: Below 1500 ft RA the second autopilot couples, FLARE armed is annunciated, the A/P go-around mode arms (not annunciated) and ROLL OUT arms if available.

question: Below 1500 ft RA in a dual approach, what happens if the pilot tries to override into CWS?

options.text: The override is accepted below 500 ft

explanation: In the final stages the pitch and roll axes cannot be overridden into CWS; trying to do so disengages the autopilots.

question: Between about 400 and 330 ft RA, what is done to the stabiliser?

options.text: It is trimmed further nose-up, held by the elevators
It is trimmed further nose-down, ready for the flare
It is locked in its current position

explanation: The stabiliser is trimmed an extra amount nose-up while the elevators hold the pitching moment. After a disconnect, forward column force may be needed.

question: Why is the stabiliser biased nose-up late in an autoland?

options.text: To aid the flare and make a failure pitch the nose up
To reduce the elevator load in turbulence close to the ground
To keep the nosewheel off the runway

explanation: The bias aids the flare. After a fail-passive disconnect the aircraft tends to pitch nose-up, avoiding a hard contact and helping a go-around.

question: If FLARE is not armed by about 350 ft RA, what happens?

options.text: The autopilot continues to land without a flare

explanation: If FLARE is not armed by about 350 ft RA, both autopilots disengage automatically.

question: At about what radio height does the autopilot flare start?
explanation: The flare starts at about 50 ft RA (45 ft gear altitude) and ends at touchdown. FLARE engaged is annunciated and the FD bars retract.

question: In the flare, the vertical speed is reduced from about 10–12 ft/s to about:
explanation: The flare mode replaces G/S and reduces the sink rate from around 10–12 ft/s at 50 ft to 1–2 ft/s at touchdown.

question: What is the controlling signal in the autoland flare mode?

options.text: The barometric vertical speed from the ADC
The rate of reduction of radio height

explanation: The flare uses the rate at which radio height is decreasing as its controlling signal, giving an exponential flare path.

question: At about what height does the autothrottle start retarding the thrust in an autoland?
explanation: The autothrottle begins retarding at about 27 ft RA so as to reach idle at touchdown.

question: What is gear altitude based on?

options.text: The glide slope angle and the distance to go to the threshold
Radio altitude, pitch attitude and the gear-to-antenna geometry

explanation: The pre-programmed gear altitude uses radio altitude, pitch attitude and the known distances between the landing gear, the fuselage and the radio altimeter antenna.

question: At about 5 ft gear altitude, what happens in a typical autoland?

options.text: Flare and LOC disengage; roll-out engages
The autothrottle starts to retard the thrust levers

explanation: At about 5 ft GA the flare mode disengages for the touchdown transition, LOC disengages and roll-out engages if available.

question: At about 1 ft gear altitude, to what is the pitch attitude decreased?
explanation: At about 1 ft GA the pitch attitude is decreased to 2°; at touchdown the elevators lower the nose and hold the nosewheel on the runway.

question: When does the autothrottle disengage after an autoland?

options.text: Only when the crew disengages it after taxiing clear
When reverse thrust is applied, or about 2 s after touchdown

explanation: The autothrottle disengages when reverse is applied and, regardless of reverse, about 2 seconds after touchdown.

question: When is the autoland sequence considered complete?

options.text: When the autothrottle disengages after touchdown
When the crew disengages the automatic flight control system

explanation: The AFCS remains on until manually disengaged by the crew, which completes the autoland sequence.

question: What does the runway alignment mode do?

options.text: Captures the localizer at long range
Yaws the aircraft onto the centreline before touchdown
Steers the aircraft along the runway after landing

explanation: Armed with the flare mode and engaged below about 100 ft, align mode uses the rudder to remove the drift angle, aligning the aircraft with the runway: de-crabbing.

question: When does the runway alignment mode typically engage?
explanation: Align mode is typically armed with the flare mode and engaged below about 100 ft. From 1500 ft the yaw channel computes the difference between heading and track.

question: What does the roll-out mode give?

options.text: Ground steering commands to follow the localizer centreline
Braking commands to stop the aircraft on the runway

explanation: Roll-out gives steering commands on the ground in proportion to localizer deviation, either on a para-visual display or to the rudder and nosewheel steering.

question: What is a para-visual display?

options.text: A head-up display of the runway
A rotating "barber's pole" showing steering guidance
A strip of runway lights used in low visibility
A display of the radio altitude

explanation: The PVD is a rotating barber's pole indicator giving left or right steering guidance during the roll-out.

question: What does the autopilot go-around mode require?
explanation: The A/P go-around needs dual autopilot operation and arms when FLARE armed is annunciated.

question: When can the autopilot go-around mode not be engaged?

options.text: When LAND 3 is annunciated on the approach
Before FLARE is armed, or after touchdown is sensed

explanation: The A/P GA mode cannot be engaged before flare arm is annunciated or after the autopilot senses touchdown.

question: If TO/GA is pressed after touchdown but before the autothrottle disengages, what happens?

options.text: The A/Ps disengage; the A/Ts may give GA thrust
The autopilot flies the go-around normally from the runway

explanation: The autopilots disengage and the autothrottles may command go-around thrust, with the go-around flown manually.

question: In an autopilot go-around, what speed is commanded?
explanation: The MCP speed blanks and the airspeed cursors show the AFDS commanded speed, the flap manoeuvring speed.

question: What initial pitch attitude does the autopilot command in a go-around?
explanation: The thrust levers advance to reduced GA N1 and the autopilot commands 15° nose-up, then holds the flap manoeuvring speed once a set climb rate is reached.

question: In autopilot go-around mode, which roll control is used?

options.text: A turn on to the published missed approach heading
Wings level, with no track hold
The ground track at engagement is held

explanation: The autopilots maintain the ground track existing when go-around mode was engaged.

question: Below 400 ft RA in autopilot go-around, how can the modes be changed?

options.text: By selecting a new roll mode on the MCP

explanation: Below 400 ft RA the autopilots must be disengaged to change pitch or roll modes from GA. Above 400 ft other modes can be selected.

question: Why can the pitch mode not be changed from autopilot GA at once?

options.text: Nose-down trim must first be added for single A/P use
The flaps must be retracted first
The roll mode must always be changed first

explanation: The pitch mode stays in GA until enough nose-down trim has been added automatically to undo the approach trim bias and allow single autopilot operation.

question: From autopilot GA, what level change normally allows a successful ALT ACQ?

options.text: Any altitude above the decision height
At least 1000 ft above the GA engagement altitude
At least 100 ft above the go-around engagement altitude
At least 3000 ft above the airfield

explanation: The transition from GA to ALT ACQ normally works if the selected altitude is at least 1000 ft above the GA engagement altitude, more with full GA thrust.

question: If the stabiliser trim is not satisfactory for single A/P use in a GA, what happens near the selected altitude?

options.text: The autothrottle reduces thrust to idle
ALT ACQ is inhibited and the A/P lights show steady red
The autopilot disengages with a flashing red light and a tone

explanation: ALT ACQ is inhibited, the A/P disengage lights show steady red and pitch remains in GA. Selecting a higher altitude or disengaging the autopilots clears the lights.

question: Which status is annunciated throughout a single autopilot ILS approach?
explanation: With one autopilot, 1 CH is annunciated for the whole approach after localizer capture.

question: Which of these is not available on a single autopilot approach?

options.text: Autothrottle speed control on the approach

explanation: Single autopilot approaches have no automatic flare and touchdown, no stabiliser trim bias and no A/P go-around. FLARE is not annunciated.

question: Which ground element of an ILS gives azimuth guidance?
explanation: The localizer gives runway azimuth guidance, the glide slope vertical guidance, and the markers or DME the distance to the threshold.

question: What has replaced marker beacons at most ILS installations?
explanation: Marker beacons have been replaced by distance measuring equipment in most installations.

question: Which antenna usually receives the localizer signal?

options.text: The same antenna as the VOR
The glide slope antenna on the nose

explanation: The localizer uses the VHF navigation band, so the same antenna as the VOR is usually used.

question: What is runway visual range?

options.text: The visibility reported in the METAR
The length of runway visible from the threshold
The range at which runway lights can be seen along the runway
The distance at which the runway can be seen from the approach

explanation: RVR is an instrumentally derived value: the range at which high-intensity lights can be seen in the direction of landing along the runway.

question: Why must a pilot allow for "slant visual range" on the approach?

options.text: The pilot looks down the glide path, not along the runway
The visibility is reported in statute miles, not metres
The RVR is measured in metres, not feet

explanation: The pilot's line of sight on the approach is down the glide path, not along the runway, so visual cues can differ from what the RVR suggests.

question: What is the decision height limit for a category I approach?

options.text: Lower than 100 ft or no DH

explanation: Category I has a DH no lower than 200 ft with visibility not less than 800 m or RVR not less than 550 m.

question: What is the minimum RVR for a category I approach?
explanation: Category I needs RVR not less than 550 m, or visibility not less than 800 m, with a DH not lower than 200 ft.

question: Which describes a category II operation?

options.text: DH not lower than 200 ft, and RVR at least 550 m
DH below 200 ft but not below 100 ft, RVR at least 300 m
No DH and no RVR limit
DH below 100 ft or none, RVR at least 175 m

explanation: Category II has a DH lower than 200 ft but not lower than 100 ft, with RVR not less than 300 m.

question: Which describes a category IIIA operation?

options.text: No DH and no RVR limit
DH below 200 ft, RVR at least 300 m
DH below 50 ft or none, and RVR from 50 to 175 m
DH below 100 ft or none, RVR at least 175 m

explanation: Category IIIA has a DH lower than 100 ft or no DH, and RVR not less than 175 m.

question: Which describes a category IIIB operation?

options.text: DH below 200 ft, RVR at least 300 m
No DH and no RVR limit
DH below 50 ft or none, RVR below 175 m but at least 50 m
DH below 100 ft, RVR at least 175 m

explanation: Category IIIB has a DH lower than 50 ft or no DH, and RVR less than 175 m but not less than 50 m.

question: Which describes a category IIIC operation?

options.text: No DH and no RVR limitation
DH at 200 ft, RVR at least 550 m
DH below 100 ft, RVR at least 175 m
DH below 50 ft, RVR at least 50 m

explanation: Category IIIC has no decision height and no runway visual range limitation.

question: Does "all weather operations" mean no weather can stop a landing?

options.text: No; it applies only to take-off
Yes; autoland works in any weather conditions at all
No; wind limits and runway state still apply
Yes, if the runway is category III

explanation: No system can land beyond the certified wind limits, which depend on controllability and strength, nor on a runway unfit because of water, slush or ice.

question: In which band, and at which wavelength, does the ILS localizer operate?
explanation: The localizer uses VHF (about 108–112 MHz), wavelengths of a few metres. The glide slope uses UHF (about 329–335 MHz), decimetric wavelengths.
